question: Discuss the relevance of each element in a Business Intelligence Environment.
student_answer: Business intelligence design
model_answer: Data from the business environment: Businesses must deal with both structured and unstructured data from many different sources, including big data. The data need to be integrated and organized so that they can be analyzed and used by human decision-makers. Business intelligence infrastructure: The underlying foundation of business intelligence is a powerful database system that captures all the relevant data to operate the business.  The data may be stored in transactional databases or combined and integrated into an enterprise-data warehouse or series of interrelated data marts. Business analytics toolset: A set of software tools used to analyze data and produce reports, respond to questions posed by managers, and track the progress of the business using key indicators of performance. Managerial users and methods: Managers impose order on the analysis of data using a variety of managerial methods that define strategic business goals and specify how progress will be measured. Without strong senior management oversight, business analytics can produce a great deal of information, reports, and online screens that focus on the wrong matters and divert attention from the real issues. Delivery platform—MIS, DSS, ESS: The results from business intelligence and analytics are delivered to managers and employees in a variety of ways, depending on what they need to know to perform their jobs.  One suite of hardware and software tools in the form of a business intelligence and analytics package is able to integrate all this information and bring it to managers’ desktop or mobile platforms. User interface: Businesspeople are no longer tied to their desks and desktops. They often learn quicker from a visual representation of data than from a dry report with columns and rows of information. Today’s business analytics software suites feature data visualization tools, such as rich graphs, charts, dashboards, and maps.

question: Discuss the six processes involved in project scope management as applicable to the proposed WAN project
student_answer: Planning Scope Management: This involves determining procedures, policies and documentation that will be used for planning, executing and controlling changes to project scope. The output is the scope management plan.
model_answer: i. Planning scope management: It involves determining how the project’s scope and requirements will be managed. The project team reviews information and uses expert judgment and meetings to help create a scope management plan and requirements management plan. ii. Collecting requirements: It involves defining and documenting the features and functions of the products as well as the processes used for creating them. This is often the most difficult process in scope management. A major consequence of not defining requirements well is rework, which can consume up to half of the project costs. Questionnaires and surveys can be efficient ways to collect requirements as long as key stakeholders provide honest and thorough information. Observation can also be a good technique for collecting requirements, especially for projects that involve improving work processes and procedures. For software development projects, prototyping and document analysis are common techniques for collecting requirements. iii. Defining scope: This involves reviewing the scope management plan, project charter, requirements documents, and organizational process assets to create a scope statement, adding more information as requirements are developed and change requests are approved. Outputs of scope definition are the project scope statement and updates to project documents. Key inputs for preparing the project scope statement include the project charter, scope management plan, requirements documentation, and organizational process assets such as policies and procedures related to scope statements, as well as project files and lessons learned from previous, similar projects. A project charter provides a basis for further defining the project scope. The charter describes the high-level scope, time, and cost goals for the project objectives and success criteria. iv. Create a work breakdown structure: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented grouping of the work involved in a project that defines its total scope. Creating the WBS involves subdividing the major project deliverables into smaller, more manageable components. Outputs include a scope baseline (which includes a WBS and a WBS dictionary) and updates to project documents. A WBS is often depicted as a task-oriented tree of activities, similar to an organizational chart. WBS in chart form helps the project manager to visualize the whole project and all of its main parts. A WBS dictionary is a document that provides detailed information about each WBS item. v. Validating scope: This involves formalizing acceptance of the project deliverables. Key project stakeholders, such as the customer and sponsor for the project, inspect and then formally accept the deliverables during this process. If the deliverables are not acceptable, the customer or sponsor usually requests changes. The outputs of this process are accepted deliverables, change requests, work performance information, and updates to project documents. vi. Controlling scope: This involves controlling changes to project scope throughout the life of the project—a challenge on many IT projects. At times, scope changes often influence the team’s inability to meet project time and cost goals, so project managers must carefully weigh the costs and benefits of scope changes. The outputs of this process are work performance information, change requests, and updates to the project management plan, project documents, and organizational process assets.

Ways / methods that it can be created are: Top-down Approach: This is when the project is divided into large components and later broken down into smaller components, Bottom-top Approach: This is when the project is divided into smaller components and then aggregated into large components, Mind Mapping: This is when the project scope is represented as a flowchart and the components are lines showing the relationship between them.
model_answer: i. Planning scope management: It involves determining how the project’s scope and requirements will be managed. The project team reviews information and uses expert judgment and meetings to help create a scope management plan and requirements management plan. ii. Collecting requirements: It involves defining and documenting the features and functions of the products as well as the processes used for creating them. This is often the most difficult process in scope management. A major consequence of not defining requirements well is rework, which can consume up to half of the project costs. Questionnaires and surveys can be efficient ways to collect requirements as long as key stakeholders provide honest and thorough information. Observation can also be a good technique for collecting requirements, especially for projects that involve improving work processes and procedures. For software development projects, prototyping and document analysis are common techniques for collecting requirements. iii. Defining scope: This involves reviewing the scope management plan, project charter, requirements documents, and organizational process assets to create a scope statement, adding more information as requirements are developed and change requests are approved. Outputs of scope definition are the project scope statement and updates to project documents. Key inputs for preparing the project scope statement include the project charter, scope management plan, requirements documentation, and organizational process assets such as policies and procedures related to scope statements, as well as project files and lessons learned from previous, similar projects. A project charter provides a basis for further defining the project scope. The charter describes the high-level scope, time, and cost goals for the project objectives and success criteria. iv. Create a work breakdown structure: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented grouping of the work involved in a project that defines its total scope. Creating the WBS involves subdividing the major project deliverables into smaller, more manageable components. Outputs include a scope baseline (which includes a WBS and a WBS dictionary) and updates to project documents. A WBS is often depicted as a task-oriented tree of activities, similar to an organizational chart. WBS in chart form helps the project manager to visualize the whole project and all of its main parts. A WBS dictionary is a document that provides detailed information about each WBS item. v. Validating scope: This involves formalizing acceptance of the project deliverables. Key project stakeholders, such as the customer and sponsor for the project, inspect and then formally accept the deliverables during this process. If the deliverables are not acceptable, the customer or sponsor usually requests changes. The outputs of this process are accepted deliverables, change requests, work performance information, and updates to project documents. vi. Controlling scope: This involves controlling changes to project scope throughout the life of the project—a challenge on many IT projects. At times, scope changes often influence the team’s inability to meet project time and cost goals, so project managers must carefully weigh the costs and benefits of scope changes. The outputs of this process are work performance information, change requests, and updates to the project management plan, project documents, and organizational process assets.

Collect Requirements: This involves managing project requirements that reflect on stake holders needs.Define Scope: this involves Developing a written scope statement of the project for future actions.
model_answer: i. Planning scope management: It involves determining how the project’s scope and requirements will be managed. The project team reviews information and uses expert judgment and meetings to help create a scope management plan and requirements management plan. ii. Collecting requirements: It involves defining and documenting the features and functions of the products as well as the processes used for creating them. This is often the most difficult process in scope management. A major consequence of not defining requirements well is rework, which can consume up to half of the project costs. Questionnaires and surveys can be efficient ways to collect requirements as long as key stakeholders provide honest and thorough information. Observation can also be a good technique for collecting requirements, especially for projects that involve improving work processes and procedures. For software development projects, prototyping and document analysis are common techniques for collecting requirements. iii. Defining scope: This involves reviewing the scope management plan, project charter, requirements documents, and organizational process assets to create a scope statement, adding more information as requirements are developed and change requests are approved. Outputs of scope definition are the project scope statement and updates to project documents. Key inputs for preparing the project scope statement include the project charter, scope management plan, requirements documentation, and organizational process assets such as policies and procedures related to scope statements, as well as project files and lessons learned from previous, similar projects. A project charter provides a basis for further defining the project scope. The charter describes the high-level scope, time, and cost goals for the project objectives and success criteria. iv. Create a work breakdown structure: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented grouping of the work involved in a project that defines its total scope. Creating the WBS involves subdividing the major project deliverables into smaller, more manageable components. Outputs include a scope baseline (which includes a WBS and a WBS dictionary) and updates to project documents. A WBS is often depicted as a task-oriented tree of activities, similar to an organizational chart. WBS in chart form helps the project manager to visualize the whole project and all of its main parts. A WBS dictionary is a document that provides detailed information about each WBS item. v. Validating scope: This involves formalizing acceptance of the project deliverables. Key project stakeholders, such as the customer and sponsor for the project, inspect and then formally accept the deliverables during this process. If the deliverables are not acceptable, the customer or sponsor usually requests changes. The outputs of this process are accepted deliverables, change requests, work performance information, and updates to project documents. vi. Controlling scope: This involves controlling changes to project scope throughout the life of the project—a challenge on many IT projects. At times, scope changes often influence the team’s inability to meet project time and cost goals, so project managers must carefully weigh the costs and benefits of scope changes. The outputs of this process are work performance information, change requests, and updates to the project management plan, project documents, and organizational process assets.

In the process of developing the solutions, risk can be identified, both known and unknown and can be mitigated. - Delphi technique: This involves a meeting with system, experts and professionals to predict unknown and known risk that may arise in the project. - Meetings: This involves having a thorough discussion between project managers, customers, stakeholders, users and workers to identify and mitigate known and unknown risk. In this meeting, they go over the project plan and share opinions.
model_answer: i. Brainstorming is a technique by which a group attempts to generate ideas or find a solution for a specific problem by amassing ideas spontaneously and without judgment. ii. Delphi Technique is used to derive a consensus among a panel of experts who make predictions about future developments. It Provides independent and anonymous input regarding future events and uses repeated rounds of questioning and written responses and avoids the biasing effects possible in oral methods, such as brainstorming. iii. Interviewing is a fact-finding technique for collecting information in face-to-face, phone, e-mail, or instant-messaging discussions. iv. SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) can also be used during risk identification. It helps identify the broad negative and positive risks that apply to a project.

question: Discuss the four components of project communication management.
student_answer: Communication with team: This is a component of project communication. It ensures adequate progress and prevents schedule slips.
model_answer: i.Communication plan: communication plan management is the process of gathering and analyzing project stakeholder information and requirements to develop an appropriate communication approach for the project.The project communication management plan outlines how to achieve the project communication objectives.The project manager develop communication plan and lines of the communication plan should show reporting authority. ii. Project meetings: Project meetings are an important forum for the manager to lead and manage the project participants. Some managers prefers informal adhoc  meetings while others prefers formal structured meetings. There are five basic reasons for holding a meeting: Project initiation start-up meeting – the purpose is to formally lunch the project. The attendees include the project sponsor, the project team members, contractors, suppliers, consultants and key stakeholders. Problem solving workshop – this enable the project team members to use their creative and innovative skills to brainstorm problems, generate ideas, options and alternatives. Decision-making meeting – the purpose is gain collective support and commitment from the project team for a certain course of action. Project progress meeting – progress meeting are generally schedule (weekly, monthly or quarterly) to monitor progress and guide the project to a successful completion. Handover meeting – the handover meeting formally hands over the project from the project manager to the client (project sponsor) for operation. iii. Project reporting: Project reporting is one of the mechanisms used for collecting and distributing project related information. Types of project reports: Progress status reports – simply quantifies the position of the project. It might be specific focusing on the key areas of the project, such as time, cost and quality. Variance reports – it quantifies the difference between the actual and planned performance. Progress Reports – progress report informs project manager of the current position and direction of the project. Exception Reports  - exception reports are designed to flag an occurrence which is outside predetermined control limits. For example, all the deliveries are due the following week. This would focus on the essential deliveries that could disrupts the work and resource planning. iv. Document control: Document control is an information management system used by the project manager to control the generation, distribution and storage of important documents. it is project manager’s responsibility to ensure that the project has a complying document control system and to appoint a document controller. A list of document to be controlled should be developed in conjunction with the key stakeholders; and to ensure conformance to below practices: Generation – the document to be controlled should be generated, changed and approved in the agreed manner by the nominated people. Circulation -  the controlled documents should be circulated in the agreed manner. For example, through electronic means and ensure receipt of documents. Audit – this ensure that there is audit trail of transmittal and the controlled document have been sent to right people and acknowledged. Storage – the controlled documents need to be securely archived for safekeeping and indexed for ease of retrieval.
